title: Sharpness of Resonance and Quality Factor
short_intro: The sharpness of resonance quantifies how rapidly the amplitude or energy of a driven damped oscillator drops as the driving frequency deviates from the natural frequency. It is inversely proportional to the damping coefficient and directly proportional to the quality factor Q.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of resonance, condition for amplitude resonance, effect of damping on resonance curves, and fundamental frequency matching.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of amplitude and velocity resonance frequencies, half-power bandwidth, quality factor Q, phase lag variation, and sharpness calculations in LCR circuits and mechanical systems.

prerequisites: Damped harmonic motion and differential equations

concept_notes.heading: Amplitude Resonance and Frequency
bullets: In a forced damped oscillator governed by m(d²x/dt²) + r(dx/dt) + sx = F_0 cos(ωt), the steady-state amplitude depends on the driving frequency ω.
The amplitude resonance frequency ω_r is given by ω_r = ω_0² - 2(γ/m)², where ω_0 is the undamped natural frequency and γ = r/2m is the damping factor.
For very light damping (γ << ω_0), the amplitude resonance frequency approximately equals the natural frequency ω_0.

concept_notes.heading: Sharpness and Quality Factor Q
bullets: The sharpness of resonance is measured by the Quality Factor (Q), defined as Q = ω_r / (ω_2 - ω_1), where (ω_2 - ω_1) is the full width at half maximum (bandwidth) of the power-frequency curve.
Higher Q-factor implies lower damping, leading to a narrower resonance peak and a sharper resonance.
Q can also be expressed as 2π (Energy stored / Energy dissipated per cycle).

concept_notes.heading: Phase Relations at Resonance
bullets: At exact resonance (ω = ω_0), the phase difference between the driving force and the displacement is exactly π/2 radians (90°).
Below resonance (ω < ω_0), the oscillator is stiffness-controlled and the phase lag approaches 0°.
Above resonance (ω > ω_0), the oscillator is mass-controlled and the phase lag approaches π radians (180°).

concept_notes.heading: Velocity Resonance vs Amplitude Resonance
bullets: Velocity resonance occurs strictly when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency (ω = ω_0), independent of the damping coefficient.
At velocity resonance, the impedance of the system is purely resistive, and the velocity is in phase with the driving force.
Amplitude resonance occurs at a slightly lower frequency than velocity resonance due to the frequency-dependent stiffness term.

derivations.title: Derivation of Resonance Amplitude
derivations.conditions: Steady-state forced oscillations with damping coefficient r and driving force F_0 cos(ωt)
steps: Write the equation of motion: m(d²x/dt²) + r(dx/dt) + sx = F_0 cos(ωt).
Assume a steady-state solution x(t) = A cos(ωt - φ), substitute into the equation, and equate coefficients of sin(ωt) and cos(ωt).
Solve for the amplitude A to obtain A = (F_0/m) / sqrt((omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4gamma^2omega^2), where γ = r/2m and ω_0^2 = s/m.
Differentiate A with respect to ω and set dA/dω = 0 to find the frequency of maximum amplitude: ω_r = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2gamma^2).

derivations.title: Derivation of Half-Power Bandwidth and Q-Factor
derivations.conditions: Lightly damped oscillator where γ is small compared to ω_0
steps: The kinetic energy or average power absorbed is proportional to the square of the velocity amplitude or proportional to A^2.
Half-power points occur where the average power drops to half of its maximum value, corresponding to A = A_max / sqrt(2).
This condition reduces to (omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4gamma^2omega^2 approx 2(4gamma^2omega_0^2) near resonance.
Solving for the two frequencies ω_1 and ω_2 yields the bandwidth Δω = ω_2 - ω_1 approx 2gamma = r/m.
derivations.result: Q = omega_0 / Deltaomega = omega_0 m / r

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resonance Curves for Different Damping Levels
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of Amplitude A versus Driving Frequency ω featuring three distinct curves for low, medium, and high damping (γ_1 < γ_2 < γ_3). Show sharp peaks at low damping and broader, lower peaks shifted to the left for higher damping.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As damping increases, the peak height decreases, the resonance frequency shifts to lower values, and the resonance curve becomes wider (less sharp).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in MCQs to identify which curve corresponds to minimum damping or highest Q-factor.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Lag vs Driving Frequency
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sigmoidal curve plotting phase φ against ω/ω_0. The curve starts at 0° at low frequencies, passes through exactly 90° (π/2) at ω = ω_0, and approaches 180° (π) at high frequencies.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the transition from stiffness control to mass control, with the steepest slope occurring for small damping values.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual questions regarding the phase relationship at resonance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Acoustic Resonance Apparatus (Kundt's Tube / Resonance Column)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing a tuning fork placed over a vertical water column tube, noting resonance lengths l_1 and l_2 for fundamental and overtone frequencies.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allows determination of sound velocity in air and observation of sharp acoustic resonance peaks when air column length matches quarter-wavelength multiples.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Laboratory physics practical questions and numericals on end corrections.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 0.5 kg executes forced oscillations under a periodic force. If the natural frequency is 10 rad/s and the damping constant is 0.2 kg/s, calculate the quality factor Q of the system.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: m = 0.5 kg, ω_0 = 10 rad/s, r = 0.2 kg/s.
Recall the formula for Q-factor in terms of mass, natural frequency, and damping coefficient: Q = (omega_0 m) / r.

solved_numericals.question: An LCR series circuit has inductance L = 2 H, capacitance C = 2 μF, and resistance R = 10 Ω. Calculate the resonance frequency, the quality factor Q, and the half-power bandwidth in Hz.
solution_steps: Calculate angular resonance frequency ω_0 = 1 / sqrt(LC) = 1 / sqrt(2 \times 2 \times 10^-6) = 1 / sqrt(4 \times 10^-6) = 1000 / 2 = 500 rad/s.
Calculate bandwidth in angular frequency: Δω = ω_0 / Q = 500 / 100 = 5 rad/s.
Convert bandwidth to frequency in Hz: Δf = Δω / (2π) = 5 / (2 × 3.1416) approx 0.796 Hz.
solved_numericals.answer: Resonance frequency = 500 rad/s, Q = 100, Bandwidth = 0.796 Hz

solved_numericals.question: A mechanical oscillator has a natural frequency of 200 rad/s and a bandwidth of 4 rad/s. If the driving force amplitude is 10 N and the mass is 1 kg, find the maximum amplitude at resonance.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: ω_0 = 200 rad/s, Δω = 4 rad/s, F_0 = 10 N, m = 1 kg.
Find the damping constant r using bandwidth: Δω = r / m ⇒ r = m \times Δω = 1 \times 4 = 4 kg/s.

Use the maximum amplitude formula at resonance: A_{max} = F_0 / (2mgammasqrt{omega_0^2 - gamma^2}). Since γ << ω_0, approximate A_{max} approx F_0 / (2mgammaomega_0) or use exact formula A_{max} = 10 / (2 \times 1 \times 2 \times sqrt{200^2 - 2^2}) approx 10 / (4 \times 200) = 10 / 800 = 0.0125 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Linearity assumption: Restoring force is strictly proportional to displacement (Hooke's law) and damping force is linear with velocity (F_d = -r v).
Steady-state condition: Transient terms have completely decayed, leaving only the steady forced oscillation response.
Light damping approximation (γ << ω_0) is frequently invoked for analytical simplification of resonance width and Q-factor relations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Amplitude resonance occurs exactly at the natural frequency ω_0 for all damped systems.
common_misconceptions.correct: Amplitude resonance occurs at ω_r = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2gamma^2), which is slightly lower than ω_0.
common_misconceptions.why: The damping term introduces a frequency shift in the denominator of the amplitude response function.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A higher Q-factor means a wider resonance peak covering a broader frequency range.
common_misconceptions.correct: A higher Q-factor means a narrower, sharper resonance peak with a smaller bandwidth.
common_misconceptions.why: Q is inversely proportional to bandwidth (Q = ω_0 / Δω).

common_misconceptions.wrong: At resonance, the phase difference between force and displacement is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: At resonance (ω = ω_0), the phase difference is exactly 90° (π/2 radians).
common_misconceptions.why: Displacement lags velocity by 90° and velocity is in phase with force at resonance, making displacement lag force by 90°.

quick_revision: Sharpness of resonance is directly quantified by the Quality Factor Q = ω_0 / Δω.
Amplitude resonance frequency is ω_r = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2gamma^2), whereas velocity resonance occurs strictly at ω_ = ω_0.
At resonance, phase lag between driving force and displacement is π/2.
Half-power bandwidth is equal to 2γ or r/m for light damping.
